title: AI Comes for Nursing
content:
AI Comes for Nursing
By Katie J. Wells and Tina M. Park
SUSAN IS FICTIONAL. But the pieces of her story are not. Her day reflects a composite of the experiences of real-world nurses with new AI technologies. In this report, we examine these experiences and document how nurses have unexpectedly found themselves on the frontlines of the AI industry.
AI in healthcare is often presented by industry insiders and media reporters as an unambiguous public good—and a use case that legitimizes AI’s broader social value. But there is limited evidence about how AI tools are actually integrated into healthcare settings, how risks are distributed, and who bears the costs. Little is also known about how AI tools will result in actual cost savings and additional revenue for healthcare providers.
This gap is the subject of our report. Here, we explore how nursing work is shaped by the integration of new AI tools. We show how nurses are witnessing, engaging, and, in some cases, resisting an experimental push by AI firms to put an unprecedented number of AI tools into patient care. We analyze how nurses are often expected to integrate untested AI tools into their work with no guidance about who is responsible when a tool makes an error.1National Nurses United, “National Nurses United Survey Finds A.I. Technology Degrades and Undermines Patient Safety,” press release, May 15, 2024, (<)a href='https://www.nationalnursesunited.org/press/national-nurses-united-survey-finds-ai-technology-undermines-patient-safety' target='_blank' rel='noreferrer noopener'(>)https://www.nationalnursesunited.org/press/national-nurses-united-survey-finds-ai-technology-undermines-patient-safety(<)/a(>); Hilke Schellmann, “AI Is Entering Health Care, and Nurses Are Being Asked to Trust It,” (<)em(>)Scientific American(<)/em(>), February 17, 2026.
In the process, we build an inventory of AI tools that a nurse encounters in a typical day. Then, we examine in depth three AI technologies: a scheduling mechanism, a patient-monitoring device, and a charting application. From these analyses, we argue that the rapid, haphazard, and seemingly covert integration of AI into healthcare is reorganizing the nursing workplace with significant risks for workers and patients alike. We conclude that it is not enough to examine the impact of an AI tool through the narrow aperture of whether it works according to a set of technical benchmarks.
AI in Brief
“AI” is best understood as a marketing term rather than a coherent set of technologies, and has shape shifted meaning over its near 70 year history. Today, it generally refers to systems that use large amounts of data and computing power to identify statistical patterns, which they then use to classify, predict, or generate new content.
In this report, we build our inventory of AI from the tools that nurses identified in focus groups and from our review of industry and news sources, refined it with workshop feedback, and organized it by what the tools do in the workplace.
Many of these tools rely on machine learning, including predictive systems that classify and forecast as well as generative systems such as LLMs. We excluded long standing scoring tools, such as the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and the Braden scale, which assign points according to fixed expert-set criteria rather than relying on statistical models that learn patterns from data and generate probabilistic prediction.

report.summary: AI Now Institute report finds nurses are being pushed to use untested AI scheduling, monitoring and charting tools with unclear accountability, risking patient safety and reorganizing healthcare work.
report.background: Healthcare AI is often marketed as an unambiguous public good that legitimizes the broader AI industry. But the AI Now Institute report argues there is limited evidence about how these tools are actually integrated into clinical settings, how risks are distributed, who bears the costs, and whether promised savings or revenue materialize. Nurses, who make up a huge share of the US healthcare workforce, are described as unexpected frontlines of this experimental push. The report builds an inventory of AI tools nurses encounter in a typical day and examines three in depth: a scheduling mechanism, a patient-monitoring device and a charting application. It also challenges the nursing-shortage narrative often used to justify automation, noting the US has more than seven million licensed registered and practical nurses.
key_points: The report documents a gap between healthcare AI hype and evidence. Little is known about how tools are integrated, how risks are distributed, who bears costs, or whether promised savings and revenue materialize. Nurses are often expected to use untested systems without clear guidance on who is responsible when a tool makes an error.

Researchers inventory the AI tools a nurse may encounter in a typical day and analyze three in depth: a scheduling mechanism, a patient-monitoring device and a charting application. These examples show how AI reshapes clinical workflows, labor conditions and accountability in everyday nursing work.

The report challenges the nursing-shortage narrative used to justify automation. The US has more than seven million licensed registered and practical nurses, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects about 180,800 registered-nurse openings each year through 2035, with healthcare a major source of job growth.

The authors argue that rapid, haphazard and sometimes covert AI integration is reorganizing nursing workplaces with significant risks for workers and patients. They conclude that judging an AI tool only by technical benchmarks is insufficient; workplace power, labor conditions and patient safety must be part of evaluation.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report pushes back on healthcare as a frictionless showcase for AI and raises reputational and regulatory risk if vendors cannot show clinical validation, transparency and accountability. For developers, it signals that clinical tools need audit logs, human oversight, clear escalation paths, workflow co-design with nurses and evidence beyond benchmark accuracy. Hospitals and procurement teams may face pressure to disclose AI use and assign liability. For regular users and patients, the stakes are direct: scheduling, monitoring and charting systems can affect staffing, alerts and care records. The report suggests nurses and patients should ask who is accountable when AI errs and whether frontline workers had a say in deployment.
report.tools: For follow-up, read the AI Now Institute report, National Nurses United's 2024 AI survey and Scientific American's coverage of nurses and healthcare AI. To explore clinical informatics infrastructure, examine open-source projects such as OpenMRS and openEHR, which illustrate how health data and records are structured. Also watch nurse-led AI evaluation frameworks and hospital procurement transparency efforts; these are useful for assessing whether scheduling, monitoring and charting tools include accountability, auditability and frontline input.
